members.details: Startup may have to wait for the worker to load, or for room in the pool, before your constructor runs.

callouts.body: Every `spawn` creates a new, independent instance. To share one instance, clone its client.

sections.code:
let counter = fusor_worker::spawn::<Counter>(&owner, 0).await?; // runs Counter::new(0) on a worker
let value = counter.add(3).await?;                              // runs add(3) there and gives you 3
counter.close().await?;                                         // shuts the worker down
sections.note: `Worker` is the trait that the annotation implements for your type. You never implement it yourself. You only name it to write out the client type: `<Counter as fusor_worker::Worker>::Client`.

links.label: Spawn a service and get its client

sections.title: Client
sections.body: The client is what you get when you await `spawn`. It has a method for each public method you wrote, and every call runs on the worker against the same retained state.

api.from: Awaiting a `Spawn`. Fusor generates the type, so there’s nothing to import. To write it out, use `<Counter as fusor_worker::Worker>::Client`.

members.name: .your_method(input)
members.text: Has the same name and input as the method you wrote. It returns a job, so you can add progress or cancellation to each call before you await it.
members.details:
Your method takes `&mut self`, but the client’s takes `&self`, so any clone can call it. A `TaskContext` parameter is left out, because Fusor supplies it. `T` and `E` come from your `TaskResult`, and `P` from your `TaskContext

`. Calls to one instance run one at a time, in the order they arrive.

members.name: .close()
members.text: Stops accepting calls, lets the calls already accepted finish, then releases the instance.
members.details: `close` is reserved, so none of your own methods can use that name. Closing a service that runs on a pool leaves the pool running.

members.name: .clone()
members.text: Another client for the same instance. It doesn’t copy the state.

callouts.body: Dropping every client isn’t a reliable way to stop a service, because a pool can keep it alive. Call `close()`, or let the owner that spawned it go away.

sections.language: Rust · what you write and what you call

links.label: Methods run one at a time

sections.title: Pool::new
sections.body: `Pool::new` starts building a pool: a fixed set of threads that share memory, for heavy or parallel work. It returns a `PoolInit`. Set limits on it if you want to, then await it to get the running `Pool`.

api.from: `Pool::new(&owner)`. Pools need a threaded build, and a page served with cross-origin isolation: see Building and hosting workers.

members.name: .max_threads(count)
members.text: How many compute threads to start. The default is 4, or fewer on a device that reports fewer cores. It must be at least 1.
members.signature: pub fn max_threads(self, count: usize) -> Self

members.name: .max_async_jobs(count)
members.text: How many operations may run at once on the coordinator thread. The default is 4, and it must be at least 1.
members.details: This counts every operation that runs on the coordinator: async tasks, stream producers, and service constructors and methods, even synchronous ones.
members.signature: pub fn max_async_jobs(self, count: usize) -> Self

members.name: .queue_capacity(count)
members.text: How many operations may wait for a free slot before new ones fail with `QueueFull`. The default is 64, and `0` means nothing waits.
members.details: The same number separately limits how many `compute` calls may wait.
members.signature: pub fn queue_capacity(self, count: usize) -> Self

members.name: .cancel_on(&token)
members.text: Stops startup when `token` is cancelled.
members.details: Neither this nor the handle affects a pool that has already started.
members.signature: pub fn cancel_on(self, token: &CancellationToken) -> Self

members.name: .cancellation_handle()
members.text: A handle that stops startup.
members.signature: pub fn cancellation_handle(&self) -> CancellationHandle

members.name: .await
members.text: Starts the coordinator and every compute thread, and finishes when all of them are ready.
members.details: It fails with `Unsupported` when the page can’t use shared memory. Check `capabilities()` first if you want to explain that to the user.

callouts.body: A bad limit such as `max_threads(0)` doesn’t fail on the spot. It comes back as `InvalidConfiguration` when you await.

sections.title: Pool
sections.body: A `Pool` is a running set of threads: one coordinator for async code, and several compute threads for heavy synchronous work, all sharing one memory. Put jobs, streams and services on it with `.on(&pool)`.

members.name: .threads()
members.text: How many compute threads started, not counting the coordinator.
members.signature: pub fn threads(&self) -> usize

members.name: .close()
members.text: A graceful shutdown: refuse new work, let accepted work finish, then stop.
members.signature: pub fn close(&self) -> Close

members.name: .terminate()
members.text: Stops the pool immediately. Work that’s still running fails, and the pool’s shared handles stop working.
members.signature: pub fn terminate(&self)

callouts.body: Keep the `Pool` value for as long as you use the pool. Dropping it, or its owner going away, stops the pool at once, just like `terminate()`.

sections.code:
let total = summarize::run(&owner, values).on(&pool).await?; // runs in this pool
let threads = pool.threads();                                // for example, 2
pool.close().await?;                                         // let work finish, then stop
sections.note: You can’t clone a `Pool`: lend it with `&pool`. Work placed on a pool can’t outlive it.

sections.title: Shared
sections.body: `Shared<T>` is a small handle to a value kept inside a pool. Pass the handle to later calls, instead of sending a large value every time.

api.from: Call `ctx.share(value)` in pool code, and return the handle to the page. Read the value back in pool code with `ctx.resolve(&handle)`.

params.text: The type of the stored value. It must be `Send + Sync + 'static`, and it doesn’t need Serde.

members.name: .clone()
members.text: Another handle to the same value. The data isn’t copied, and `T` doesn’t have to be `Clone`.
members.details: The value stays in the pool while any handle or resolved `Arc<T>` exists and the pool is still running.
members.signature: impl<T: Send + Sync + 'static> Clone for Shared<T>

members.name: ctx.share(value)
members.text: Stores a value and returns its handle.

members.name: ctx.resolve(&handle)
members.text: Reads the value, as a read-only `Arc<T>`.
members.details:
To change shared data, put a `Mutex` or an atomic inside `T`, and don’t hold a lock across an `.await`.

A handle from another pool fails with `WrongPool`, an expired handle with `StaleShared`, and a handle of the wrong type with `SharedTypeMismatch`.

callouts.body: The page can hold, clone, drop and pass on a handle, but it can’t read the data. Only pool code can do that.
Pass a handle on its own: as a task argument, a result or a stream item. It can’t go inside a struct, tuple or `Vec` that you send, because it has no Serde implementation.

sections.code:
let data = dataset::run(&owner, 100).on(&pool).await?;         // builds the data inside the pool
let a = summarize::run(&owner, data.clone()).on(&pool).await?; // sends only the handle
let b = summarize::run(&owner, data).on(&pool).await?;         // reuses the same data

sections.title: ResultStream
sections.body: A `ResultStream` is a background call that sends back many results, a batch at a time, instead of one big reply at the end. Read it in a loop with `next().await`.

api.from: Call a stream task’s generated `stream` function, such as `batches::stream(&owner, 100)`.

params.text: The type of each item. It’s often a `Vec` of rows, so that each item is a batch.
The producer’s own error type, or `NoError`.
The type of progress update, or `()`.
`Unbound` until you choose a pool, as on `Job`.

members.name: .next().await
members.text: Gives you the next item: `Some(Ok(item))`, `Some(Err(error))`, or `None` when the stream has finished. The first call starts the producer.
members.details:
When the producer finishes, you get every item it had already sent, then `None`. When it returns an error, you get the items it had sent, then the error once, then `None`. Cancellation, the owner going away, or a crash discards any pending items and gives you a single error.

No trait import is needed. The type also implements `futures_core::Stream`, if you prefer stream combinators.
members.signature: pub async fn next(&mut self) -> Option<TaskResult<T, E>>

members.name: .buffer(batches)
members.text: How many items may be waiting for you before the producer pauses. The default is 4, and it must be at least 1.
members.signature: pub fn buffer(self, batches: usize) -> Self

members.name: .max_batch_bytes(bytes)
members.text: The largest size one item may have once encoded. The default is 1 MiB, and the maximum is 16 MiB.
members.details: An invalid value comes back as `InvalidConfiguration` from the first `next()`.
members.signature: pub fn max_batch_bytes(self, bytes: usize) -> Self

members.name: .on_progress(callback)
members.text: Receives progress updates, as on `Job`.
members.signature: pub fn on_progress(self, callback: impl FnMut(P) + 'static) -> Self

members.name: .cancel_on(&token)
members.text: Cancels the stream when `token` is cancelled.
members.signature: pub fn cancel_on(self, token: &CancellationToken) -> Self

members.name: .scope(&owner)
members.text: Also cancels the stream when a second owner goes away.
members.signature: pub fn scope(self, owner: &OwnerHandle) -> Self

members.name: .on(&pool)
members.text: Runs the producer on `pool`. You must choose a pool for a task annotated `#[task(pool, stream)]`.

members.name: .cancellation_handle()
members.text: A handle your UI can keep, to cancel the stream later.
members.signature: pub fn cancellation_handle(&self) -> CancellationHandle

callouts.body: Dropping the stream cancels it, and the producer’s next `send` fails, so it stops producing.

sections.title: StreamSender
sections.body: `StreamSender` is how a stream task sends its results. Each `send` delivers one item to the page’s `ResultStream`.

api.from: Add it as the last parameter of an async function annotated `#[fusor_worker::task(stream)]`. Fusor provides it: the page never passes it.

params.text: The item type. It must be a `Message`.

members.name: .send(item).await
members.text: Sends one item, waiting first if the page’s buffer is full. `Ok` means the item was accepted, not that the page has read it yet.
members.details: It fails with `Cancelled` when the page has cancelled or dropped the stream: pass that on with `?` to stop producing. It also fails when the item can’t be encoded, is too large, or holds an invalid shared handle.
members.signature: pub async fn send(&mut self, item: T) -> Result<(), WorkerError>

callouts.body: To send many small results efficiently, collect them into a `Vec` and send that as one item.

sections.note: A stream task returns `TaskResult<()>`, because its results go through the sender rather than the return value. An optional `TaskContext` parameter goes just before the sender.

sections.title: Close
sections.body: `Close` is a graceful shutdown for a pool or a stateful worker. When you await it, new calls are refused, calls already accepted are allowed to finish, and then it completes.

members.name: .timeout(duration)
members.text: How long to wait for accepted work to finish. The default is five seconds. Set it before you await.
members.signature: pub fn timeout(self, duration: std::time::Duration) -> Self

members.name: .await
members.text: Finishes once accepted work is done, or with `CloseTimedOut` if the deadline passes first.
members.details: Calling close again joins the same shutdown, and dropping a started `Close` doesn’t reopen anything. If a service method on a pool is still running at the deadline, callers stop waiting, but the service’s state is kept until that method returns.

callouts.body: Closing a service that runs on a pool leaves the pool running. To stop a pool immediately, call `pool.terminate()`.

sections.title: TaskResult
sections.body:
`TaskResult<T, E>` is the return type of every task, service method and constructor. It’s also what you get when you await a job.

It’s an ordinary Rust `Result`: either your value, or a `JobError` that says whether your code or Fusor failed.

api.from: You write it as the return type of your tasks and service methods.

params.text: Your own error type. Leave it out, as in `TaskResult<u64>`, when your code has no error of its own. It then defaults to `NoError`.

callouts.body: `NoError` is an enum with no values, so it can never happen. A `TaskResult<T>` can still fail with a `WorkerError`, for example when the job is cancelled.

sections.code:
#[fusor_worker::task]
pub fn total(values: Vec<u64>) -> TaskResult<u64> {           // has no error of its own
    Ok(values.into_iter().sum())
}

#[fusor_worker::task]
pub fn parse_count(text: String) -> TaskResult<u32, String> { // fails with a String
    text.parse::<u32>()
        .map_err(|error| JobError::Application(error.to_string()))
}

sections.title: JobError
sections.body: `JobError` is the error side of a `TaskResult`. It tells you whose failure it was: your code’s, or Fusor’s.

params.text: Your task’s own error type, or `NoError`.

members.name: Application(E)
members.text: An error your own code returned, of your type `E`.
members.details: Create one explicitly, usually inside `map_err`: `JobError::Application(error)`. There’s no automatic conversion from `E`, because it would conflict with the one below.

members.name: Worker(WorkerError)
members.text: A failure from Fusor: the job was cancelled, the worker crashed, a value was too large, and so on.
members.details: `?` turns a `WorkerError` into this variant for you.

callouts.body: `JobError` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a `match` on it needs a final `_` arm.

sections.note: `E` must be a `Message`, but it doesn’t have to implement `std::error::Error`: `String` works. `JobError<E>` implements `Display` when `E` does and `Error` when `E: Error + 'static`, and it always implements `Debug` and Serde’s traits.

sections.title: WorkerError
sections.body: `WorkerError` covers every failure that comes from Fusor rather than from your code. The groups below say what happened and what you can usually do about it.

api.from: Inside `JobError::Worker`, and directly from methods such as `check_cancelled`, `compute` and `send`.

members.name: Cancelled
members.text: The caller cancelled, through a token, a `CancellationHandle`, or by dropping the job. There’s usually nothing to show the user.
members.details: The worker may still have been running when this was reported.

members.name: OwnerDisposed
members.text: The owner, or an extra scope, went away: for example, because the component was removed.

members.name: Closed
members.text: The pool or service was closed before this call was accepted.

members.name: Terminated
members.text: The pool was terminated or dropped.

members.name: CloseTimedOut
members.text: A graceful close reached its deadline while this call was still running.

members.name: PoolRequired
members.text: This work needs a pool. Add `.on(&pool)`.

members.name: Unsupported { capability }
members.text: The browser lacks something the operation needs, such as shared memory. `capability` says which.
members.details: For pools, check that the page is served over HTTPS (or from localhost) with the cross-origin isolation headers.

members.name: IncompatibleArtifact
members.text: The worker files and the page come from different builds. Deploy one complete build.

members.name: WrongPool
members.text: The handle belongs to a different pool.

members.name: StaleShared
members.text: The handle no longer points at live data, for example because its pool was closed or restarted.

members.name: SharedTypeMismatch
members.text: The handle holds a different type from the one the code expected.

members.name: QueueFull { capacity }
members.text: Too many operations are already waiting. Try again later, or raise `queue_capacity`.

members.name: PayloadTooLarge { limit, actual }
members.text: A value was bigger than a size limit. Both numbers are in bytes.

members.name: InvalidConfiguration { message }
members.text: A builder setting was invalid, or was changed after the operation had started.

members.name: Encode { message }
members.text: A value couldn’t be turned into a message.

members.name: Decode { message }
members.text: A message couldn’t be turned back into a value.

members.name: Load { message }
members.text: The worker’s files couldn’t be loaded. Check the browser’s network tab and your content security policy.

members.name: Crashed { message }
members.text: Worker code panicked or trapped. Its state is gone, so create a new pool or service.

api.declaration:
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum WorkerError {
    Cancelled,
    OwnerDisposed,
    Closed,
    Terminated,
    CloseTimedOut,
    Unsupported { capability: Capability },
    PoolRequired,
    IncompatibleArtifact,
    WrongPool,
    StaleShared,
    SharedTypeMismatch,
    QueueFull { capacity: usize },
    PayloadTooLarge { limit: usize, actual: usize },
    InvalidConfiguration { message: String },
    Encode { message: String },
    Decode { message: String },
    Load { message: String },
    Crashed { message: String },
}

callouts.body: `WorkerError` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a `match` on it needs a final `_` arm.
Fusor never retries a failed call for you, because it may already have changed something. Whether to retry is your decision.

sections.note: `WorkerError` implements `Clone`, `Debug`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Display` and `Error`.

sections.title: Message
sections.body:
`Message` is the rule for anything that travels between the page and a worker: arguments, results, errors, progress updates and stream items.

You never implement it yourself. Fusor implements it for every type that qualifies.

api.from: Automatic, for owned types that implement Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` and are `Send + 'static`.

callouts.body: Deriving the Serde traits needs `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }` in your `Cargo.toml`.
`Shared<T>` is a `Message` without Serde, so it can’t be nested inside a type that you derive Serde for.

terms.text: Owned data: numbers, `bool`, `String`, `Vec<T>`, `Option<T>`, your own structs and enums that derive `Serialize` and `Deserialize`, and `Shared<T>` handles.
Borrowed data such as `&str`, plus signals, owners, DOM elements, callbacks and closures. Those belong to the page.
Each value, and each whole request or reply, can be at most 16 MiB once encoded.

sections.title: capabilities
sections.body: `capabilities()` tells you what the current browser supports, so you can explain a missing feature before you try to start a pool.

api.from: `fusor_worker::capabilities()`. It takes no arguments and returns straight away.

members.name: dedicated_workers
members.text: Ordinary workers are available.

members.name: shared_memory
members.text: Pools can run: workers are available, the page is cross-origin isolated, and shared memory exists.

members.name: hardware_parallelism
members.text: How many threads the device suggests. It’s a hint, not a promise that those cores are free.

members.name: Capability
members.text: An enum that names one feature, `DedicatedWorkers` or `SharedMemory`. It’s what `WorkerError::Unsupported` reports as missing.

title: Coherent async views
lead: Use `<Await>` to display an async result. Add `<Async>` when several results must change together.

sections.title: See why a boundary helps
sections.body:
The companion’s “Two reads, one complete view” section loads price and stock separately for product A.

Choose B: the old A view stays visible while either B read is pending, then the product name, price, and stock change together. Use browser network throttling to observe the transition.

This guide builds on components, owners, and the async crate from Async data loading.
sections.code:
# From the fusor repository root, after Installation:
fusor dev --manifest-path apps/docs/tutorial/Cargo.toml --port 8091

sections.title: Keep the selection in Rust
sections.body: The parent needs the selected product. `Price` and `Stock` each declare their own request. `<Async>` will create the coordinator automatically, so this basic version needs no boundary field.
sections.note: The complete companion also keeps an explicit boundary handle for its status and retry controls, shown below.

links.label: Complete App with the boundary fields

sections.title: Let a view update independently
sections.body:
The `Price` and `Stock` components below each use `<Await>` in their template. Render them outside `<Async>` and each updates as soon as its own read succeeds.

They use the same Rust read declaration in both modes; the surrounding HTML chooses whether to coordinate them.
sections.code:
<section>
  <Price product="{{ state.product.clone() }}"></Price>
  <Stock product="{{ state.product.clone() }}"></Stock>
</section>
sections.note:
For a direct read on the current state, write `

{{ price.as_str() }}

`. `Price` and `Stock` encapsulate that same pattern.

sections.title: Choose which elements change together
sections.body:
Wrap the product label, price, and stock in `<Async>`. They will switch from A to B together.

`<Async>` creates its own boundary; there is no `state.view` to declare for this version. Keep selection controls outside so they remain usable while loading.
sections.code: Product {{ state.product.get() }}
sections.note: Each tag constructs a separate child. `Price::from_inputs` and `Stock::from_inputs` receive their own `OwnerHandle` and pass it to the constructor that creates `browser::read`. Their product input is a shared `Signal`, so the existing children follow the selected product.

links.label: Compare async and coherent async side by side
What is owner, and where does it come from?

sections.title: Let each child declare its own read
sections.body:
Each child calls `browser::read` with three arguments: its owner, a function that reads the selected product, and an async loader.

The result is `AsyncValue<String, String, String>`: product code, response text, and error message. Declaring the read does not display it; the child’s HTML uses `<Await>` below.

sections.title: Put each resolved value in its template
sections.body:
This HTML file defines the `Price` and `Stock` templates. In the companion’s `Cargo.toml`, it is registered as `pricing = "web/pricing.html"` under `[package.metadata.fusor.components]`; `src/lib.rs` declares `mod pricing;`.

Within each `<Await>`, `let="result"` gives the successful value the local name `result`. Its type is `Rc<String>`: a shared pointer to the loaded string. Call `result.as_str()` to display its text. This local name is available only inside that `<Await>`.

The companion serves its test data from `public/data/price/{A,B}.txt` and `public/data/stock/{A,B}.txt`.

sections.title: Add status and retry controls when needed
sections.body:
For access from Rust, add view: `AsyncBoundary` to `App` and initialize it with `AsyncBoundary::coherent()`. Pass that handle to `<Async>`.

This is what the runnable companion does; automatic `<Async>` works without it. A boundary can attach to only one live region.
sections.code:
{{ format!("{:?}", state.view.status()) }}

{{ state.product.get() }}
sections.note: Import `fusor_async::AsyncBoundary` in `App`’s Rust module. For controls on just one independent result, put only that `<Await>` inside its own explicit `<Async>`. Keep status and retry controls outside the controlled region.

sections.title: Know what the reader sees on failure
sections.body:
While B loads, keep showing the complete A view. Once both B requests succeed, switch the label and both results together.

If a request fails, keep the last complete view and let the reader retry using the outside button.

Before any successful load, the region shows its authored placeholders. Old content cannot be interacted with while the replacement is pending or failed.
sections.note: Standalone `<Await>` follows the same retention rule for its own result. Separate `<Await>` views can show results from different selections; use `<Async>` if that would be misleading. Use `Resource` when you need to build your own loading, error, and editing UI.

sections.title: Where to use this today
sections.body:
Use `<Async>` and `<Await>` for read-only result views with generated bindings, component tags, `<Children>`, and `<ForEach>`. Each built-in wraps one native HTML root without creating an element.

`<Await>` may nest to express dependent reads.

Nested `<Async>` boundaries, editable controls, router outlets, external widgets, and independent islands inside these views are not supported. A browser view may use these components inside an activated island.
sections.note: `<Await>` takes `AsyncValue` from `browser::read`, not `Resource` or an arbitrary future. Each read declaration belongs to one live boundary; create separate declarations for independent views. This coordinates what appears on screen, not an atomic snapshot of your backend.

title: Coherent async behavior
lead: The detailed contract behind “keep the old view until the next one is complete.” Read this when choosing loading, error, and interaction behavior.

sections.title: AsyncBoundary::coherent()
sections.body:
Creates an optional handle for `<Async boundary="{{ state.view }}">`. Use it for status and retry controls; plain `<Async>` creates one automatically.

`browser::read` declares each `AsyncValue` and `<Await>` consumes its successful result. The parent does not have to gather its children’s futures.

sections.title: status() and retry()
sections.body:
`boundary.status()` reactively reports a `BoundaryStatus`. Before a region attaches, it is `Detached`. While a candidate view loads, it is `Pending`; a complete published view is `Ready`.

`Error(String)` carries a loader failure. `Faulted(String)` instead means preparing or committing the view failed. `Disposed` means the boundary’s lifetime ended.

Keep status and retry controls outside the region so they remain usable while that region blocks interactions.
sections.note: `retry()` retries failed reads while keeping compatible successful results. A new selection supersedes the previous attempt. Faulted is distinct from a loader error; inspect the reported diagnostic and correct the failed setup.

sections.title: Failure and interaction states in detail
sections.body:
On the first load, unresolved bindings show their authored placeholders until a complete view is ready. On later loads, the last complete view remains.

Pending, failed, and faulted regions block stale interactions. A failed read sets the boundary to Error; the external Retry button retries failed reads while keeping compatible successes.

New selection inputs supersede the previous attempt.
sections.note: For native HTML that should remain useful before first activation, islands can use an explicit preview. Arbitrary server HTML is not automatically treated as fulfilled async data.

sections.title: Use the first version within its boundaries
sections.body:
Use coherent regions for generated text, attributes, classes, events, and owned children or `<ForEach>` lists.

Constructors and render calculations must stay pure apart from declared reads; ordinary effects in prepared descendants wait for publication.

Keep editable controls outside the region. Nested boundaries, router outlets, foreign widget DOM, custom elements, and regions spanning independent islands are unsupported.
sections.note: This is a display-publication guarantee, not a database transaction or general rollback mechanism. Your loader, cache, authentication, and server remain application choices.

title: Routing and navigation
lead: Declare which HTML belongs at each URL. Compose nested routers through ordinary components, even when their HTML lives in another file.

sections.title: Start with two pages and a fallback
sections.body:
This example replaces the main page of the generated `my-app` from Installation. Keep its `build.rs` and existing dependencies.

Add the dependency below under `[dependencies]`. In `[package.metadata.fusor]`, add `history-fallback = ["/articles", "/missing"]`.

Create the five files below. The build discovers `web/components/pages.html`; a `template!` call in its associated Rust module connects that HTML to the page types.
sections.code: fusor-router = { version = "=0.1.1", features = ["browser"] }
sections.note: Use the same framework version as the app generated by your CLI.

sections.title: Define the state each page needs
sections.body:
`Home` and `NotFound` are unit structs: Rust types with no fields. `Article` has a `String` input called id. `#[derive(FromInputs)]` lets a component tag supply that input.

Here every captured id is a string; /articles/42 and /articles/hello both match. Validate or parse it in your own Rust constructor if you require a number.

sections.title: Give those types their HTML
sections.body:
The `<Article>` tag mounts the template marked `rust:component="Article"`. Within that template, `state.id` comes from the tag’s `id` input.

No HTML filename is inferred from the URL. The `<Route>` selects the component tag, and `template!` associates the Rust type with its HTML.

sections.title: Import the page components
sections.body: These are ordinary Rust imports. The HTML associated with this module can refer to `Home`, `Article`, and `NotFound` because those names are in this module’s scope. `App` is your root state; it happens to need no fields.

sections.title: Select the HTML for the current URL
sections.body:
`<Router>` renders the children of the best matching `<Route>`. At `/articles/42`, the `:id` segment captures `"42"`.

The attribute `let="params"` declares a local capture object inside that route. Its `params.id` field is a decoded `String` passed to `Article`. You choose the local name `params`.

A route marked `fallback` renders only when no sibling matches. Neither `<Router>` nor `<Route>` creates a wrapper element.
sections.note: `data-fusor-link` opts a real anchor into SPA navigation. Copying its URL, opening a new tab, modified clicks, targets and downloads retain browser behavior.

sections.title: Connect the Rust modules
sections.body: The `mod` declarations include the Rust files in your library. Together with the imports and `template!` calls above, they complete the setup for this example.

sections.title: Follow a complete navigation
sections.body:
Run the command below from `my-app`. Open http://127.0.0.1:8090/ and click Article 42. The article replaces the home view while the navigation remains.

Back returns to Library. Loading /articles/7 directly renders Article 7. /missing renders Page not found.
sections.code: fusor dev --port 8090

sections.title: Put a nested router in another file
sections.body:
Add a parent route ending in `/*`. It consumes its prefix and delegates the remaining path to routers inside its mounted children.

`Dashboard` is an ordinary component imported into `src/app.rs`. It can live in its own Rust module and HTML file. The root router is still the only browser-history owner.
sections.code:
<Route path="/dashboard/*">
  <Dashboard></Dashboard>
</Route>
sections.note: Also add "`/dashboard`" to `history-fallback` for direct document requests.

sections.title: Define the separate Dashboard component
sections.body: Add `mod dashboard`; to `src/lib.rs` and `use crate::dashboard::Dashboard`; to `src/app.rs`. This component has local state so you can see retention: its count survives navigation between its child routes.

sections.title: Match only the remaining path
sections.body:
At `/dashboard`, the remaining path is empty, so `path=""` matches. At `/dashboard/settings`, `path="settings"` matches. The nested fallback handles `/dashboard/unknown`.

This `<Router>` receives its prefix through component ownership, including across files. It needs no additional registration. Repeat the same pattern for deeper nesting.
sections.note: The URLs in this example assume base-path = "/". Anchors follow browser URL resolution; their href is not automatically relative to the nearest `Route`.

sections.title: Understand matching and page lifetime
sections.body:
`Route` paths accept literal segments, `:name` captures, and a final `/*` for nested routing. Literal segments take precedence over captures. An exact match takes precedence over an otherwise equal delegated pattern, regardless of declaration order. Ambiguous siblings and duplicate fallbacks are build errors.

Trailing slashes are equivalent. Captures are decoded once, after splitting the path into segments: `a%2Fb` becomes the single value `"a/b"`. A router with no match and no fallback renders nothing.
sections.code:
<Route path="/teams/:team/*" let="params">
  <Team team="{{ params.team }}"></Team>
</Route>
sections.language: HTML · Team is an application-defined component
sections.note:
Changing a captured path parameter replaces that route’s view. Changing only the remaining path of a delegated route preserves its parent view and updates the nested router. Leaving a branch disposes it; returning creates a fresh instance.

Query and fragment changes preserve matched pages. Fallbacks retain on query changes and replace on path changes. There is no hidden page cache.

sections.title: Read the current URL from Rust
sections.body:
In a component constructor, `owner` is the `OwnerHandle` supplied by `FromInputs`.

`Navigation::from_owner` finds the routing context provided before that page is constructed. `location()` is a reactive `Derived<AppUrl>`; read it in a binding or resource key to react to query changes.

A newly prepared page sees the destination URL immediately. The lookup is explicit, so components outside a router can handle its absence.

sections.title: Navigate from an event or action
sections.body:
Prefer real anchors for links. For programmatic navigation, retain `Navigation` in component state and call `navigate_url` after activation.

`NavigateOptions::default()` pushes a history entry; `replace: true` replaces the current entry. `keep_focus` and `keep_scroll` can preserve a query control’s interaction.

URLs follow browser resolution and must remain inside the same origin and configured base.
sections.code:
use fusor_router::browser::NavigateOptions;

navigation.navigate_url("/articles/42", NavigateOptions::default())?;
sections.language: Rust · after the component has activated
sections.note: The router stages a replacement before changing history or discarding the old view. Preparation errors retain the old view and URL. `last_error()` exposes listener-driven failures. Constructors should avoid unrelated side effects; arbitrary application side effects cannot be rolled back.

sections.title: Load data in the page that needs it
sections.body:
Routing selects and owns a page; data loading stays in your application. Create a `Resource` in the page’s `FromInputs` constructor with its supplied owner.

Store `Navigation.location()` when query changes should reload that resource. Leaving the page disposes its owned work. The reader example combines these APIs with loading/error UI and refresh.
sections.code:
fusor dev --package fusor-navigation --port 8093
# Open http://127.0.0.1:8093/reader/

sections.title: Make direct links work after deployment
sections.body:
The CLI dev/serve commands honor `history-fallback`. Your production host needs equivalent rules: serve `index.html` for document navigation under these prefixes, and actual 404s for missing assets and API endpoints.

At a non-root base, route patterns stay application-relative; anchors and `navigate_url` need URLs including that base. Use the configured `FUSOR_BASE_PATH` for static link helpers, or a typed `Route` with `BasePath::href` for checked link generation.
sections.code:
[package.metadata.fusor]
entry = "web/index.html"
assets = "public"
output = "dist"
base-path = "/"
history-fallback = ["/articles", "/dashboard", "/missing"]
sections.note: These are browser SPA routes. The static server’s fallback response has HTTP 200, even when a `Route` fallback displays a not-found page. SSR routing and automatic per-route bundle splitting are not included.

sections.title: Build a custom router when you need one
sections.body:
The HTML API uses `fusor_router::browser::declarative::ViewRouter` to own matching and view replacement. This is separate from the browser History API adapter, so `ViewRouter` can also serve embedded panels or a custom URL source.

`RouteView` supplies lazy view factories. `NavigationDriver` stages a transition; `PreparedNavigation` commits it. Dropping a staged transition rolls it back. Only one transition per tree can be staged at a time. Complete it synchronously before yielding to the browser, because preparation temporarily inserts inactive DOM.

The lower-level typed `Router<R>`, `Route`, and `Content` APIs remain available for integrations. Ordinary applications can use the HTML API shown above.
sections.note: `<Router>` is browser-only and cannot be declared inside coherent `<Async>` or `<Await>` regions, or in server/shared templates. A matched page may contain `<Async>` and `<Await>`. Nested routers share navigation; they do not create independent browser histories.

title: Islands
lead: Display HTML first, then start each interactive part when it is needed. Learn where the HTML comes from, what `hydrate` does, and how island state behaves.

sections.title: What is an island?
sections.body:
An island is a part of a page that already has HTML, but starts its Rust behavior separately.

Imagine a product page: the description is readable immediately, while a cart becomes interactive when the visitor reaches it. The cart is the island.

Hydration is the step that starts its browser behavior. You can keep using a normal fusor SPA without islands.
sections.note: Use islands when useful content can appear before its interactive code is needed. A normal SPA is still a good fit when most of the screen needs to be interactive together.

sections.title: Where does the HTML come from?
sections.body:
In our catalog example, Rust runs on your development machine or build service and writes the initial HTML into `index.html`. You deploy that file together with the JavaScript loader and Wasm assets.

Static hosting sends those files to visitors; it does not execute your Rust. No running Rust server is required for this build-time approach.
sections.code:
BUILD
Rust renderer → index.html + browser assets

VISIT
Static hosting sends index.html → browser displays the page

HYDRATE
Loader obtains the island’s browser code → Rust/Wasm makes it interactive
sections.note:
Some guides call this server rendering because the HTML is produced outside the browser. For this example, “HTML generated at build time” is more precise.

The renderer can also be used by a Rust server to generate HTML per request; you would integrate that server yourself. The islands build command does not create an HTTP backend.

sections.title: Choose when it becomes interactive
sections.body:
This `Cart` tag renders the registered cart view’s HTML immediately. `hydrate="visible"` asks the loader to start its browser behavior when its boundary enters the viewport.

product_id, title, and quantity are the initial inputs; `{{ 42 }}` is a Rust integer expression, while the quoted text supplies string values.
sections.code:
<Cart hydrate="visible"
      product_id="{{ 42 }}" title="Your cart" quantity="1"></Cart>
sections.language: HTML · inside the catalog’s native page template
sections.note: `Cart` is a Rust type imported by the page. Its registration connects it to `CartView` and that view’s HTML file; the setup guide shows every part. Leave this tag empty because the registered view supplies its contents. fusor wraps it in a div and generates an instance ID.

links.label: Set up the native renderer and browser bundles

sections.title: Does an island have normal reactivity?
sections.body:
Yes. Once hydrated, its browser component tree uses the same signals, computed values, event handlers, reactive lists, and owned cleanup as other fusor components. It can also load data asynchronously and use coherent async rendering.

Before hydration, there is no running browser Rust state for this island: its text is readable and native links and forms can work, but Rust handlers and reactive updates have not started.
sections.code: {{ state.quantity.get() }}
sections.language: HTML · excerpt from the cart’s shared view
sections.note: In the example, `state.quantity` is a `Signal<String>` created by `CartView::new`. Before hydration, typing edits the native input but does not update the paragraph. Hydration adopts the edited value; later edits update the signal and paragraph normally. Shared HTML needs resolved initial data; browser-only async startup uses the preview path described below.

sections.title: What can islands share?
sections.body:
Components inside one island can share signals and state normally. Separate island instances have separate state and ownership.

Their tag inputs are initial serialized values, not live connections: product_id="`{{ 42 }}`" sends the value 42, not a shared Rust signal. Updating one island does not automatically update another.
sections.code:
Within an island:
Shared signal → its components update

Between islands:
Explicit serialized event → receiving island updates its own state
sections.note: Separate Wasm bundles do not share Rust memory, signals, `Rc` handles, or closures. Use the island event APIs for messages between active islands. An inactive island has no Rust listener running; events are not a queued state store. Multiple instances can share a downloaded bundle while keeping their own state.

sections.title: Choose one hydration policy
sections.body:
Choose `hydrate="load"` to start as soon as the loader registers the instance; "visible" when it enters the viewport; "idle" when the browser has idle time (with a two-second timeout); "interaction" when the visitor uses an explicit target button; or "manual" when active Rust requests it.

These choices control when behavior starts, not whether the initial HTML is displayed.
sections.code:
<Cart hydrate="visible" hydrate:prefetch="idle"
      product_id="{{ 42 }}" title="Your cart" quantity="1"></Cart>
sections.note:
Usually `hydrate` alone is enough. Add `hydrate:prefetch` only to download code earlier: none (the default), load, visible, or idle. Prefetch does not construct state or start data reads.

Instances share downloaded code while keeping their own state. Without `hydrate`, a tag follows the ordinary component mounting API; it does not become an island.

sections.title: Use an explicit activation button
sections.body:
Name the instance with `hydrate:id` and point a native `type="button"` button at it with `hydrate:target`. The button works with mouse or keyboard before the target’s Rust runs. A second deliberate click retries failed activation.

These controls belong to the delivery loader; they do not require an already-running `App`.
sections.code:
<button type="button" hydrate:target="designer-42">Open designer</button>
<Designer hydrate="interaction" hydrate:id="designer-42"
          product_id="{{ 42 }}" title="Design a product"></Designer>
sections.language: HTML · an explicit button and its target island
sections.note: `hydrate:id` is optional for load, visible, idle, and manual, and required for interaction. It is a static, unique instance name. Use it for a manual instance when active Rust needs to look it up. An ordinary id input belongs to your props, not to the generated boundary.

sections.title: What happens to the visible HTML?
sections.body:
The default attach mode reuses the existing HTML nodes and connects their Rust behavior. Bound inputs preserve edits made before hydration. If a visitor is composing text, hydration waits until composition ends.

Use preview mode when the browser view differs from the initial HTML. The static preview stays visible while the browser view prepares. Once its initial coherent reads finish, the prepared view replaces the preview in one step.
sections.note: Native links and forms only work when their URLs and endpoints exist. Static hosting can serve the HTML, but an action such as submitting an order still needs a backend. `Island` hydration does not supply that backend.

links.label: Connect the native and browser views

sections.title: Handle a slow or failed activation
sections.body:
A failed initial preview read keeps the native preview and rejects activation. Explicit retry creates a fresh attempt. Removal or cancellation disposes pending work.

A transient Wasm download can be retried; a module evaluation or initialization failure requires a corrected build and reload. Keep fallback content meaningful while these operations are pending.

sections.title: Choose meaningful feature boundaries
sections.body:
Separate Wasm units can duplicate runtime support when several are loaded. The catalog compares separate and grouped builds of the same views.

Prefer independently used features to one unit per button.

This release does not support nested islands, server async streaming, or coherent regions across units. These are delivery tradeoffs to measure for your app.
sections.note: Start with meaningful features such as a cart or product designer. Keep tightly connected reactive components inside the same island. Each island can contain ordinary nested components; nested independent islands are not supported in this release.

sections.title: Build your first island
sections.body: The working catalog includes all the files needed to connect the initial HTML to its browser code. Continue to `Island` setup to build it and follow the Rust types, HTML templates, registrations, and Cargo configuration. Adding `hydrate` to an arbitrary SPA component alone does not create a separate browser bundle.

links.label: Set up the native renderer and browser bundles

title: Island setup
lead: Build the working catalog, then follow the files that connect its initial HTML to separately loaded Rust/Wasm. Read Islands first for the rendering and reactivity model.

sections.title: Build the working catalog first
sections.body:
The complete example lives under `examples/islands` in the framework checkout. It already has the manifests, renderer, descriptors, templates, and browser registrations.

Install Node for this build workflow, then use the CLI from Installation. The build runs the native renderer and saves the HTML; the serve command only serves the generated files.

Build the catalog and serve its output; open http://127.0.0.1:8094/. These commands run in the framework repository, not in your generated `my-app`.
sections.code:
# From the fusor repository root:
fusor build --package catalog-site --locked
fusor preview examples/islands/site/dist --port 8094
sections.note: The catalog also contains an async designer test fixture whose API responses are supplied by browser tests. The native cart/activation example runs from the static build; use `just test islands` to exercise the controlled async scenarios.

sections.title: Follow the packages through the build
sections.body: The native site links descriptors and native-renderable views. Each browser unit links the interactive view implementation it needs. A shared loader connects the resulting HTML hosts to those units. This explicit split is what avoids sending every feature in one initial Wasm bundle.
sections.code:
examples/islands/
  types/           Cart, CartProps, Designer: shared contracts
  views/           CartView: state + shared cart.html template
  cart-web/        browser registration of CartView
  designer-views/ browser designer implementation
  designer-web/   browser registration of Designer
  site/            native renderer + delivery configuration
  grouped-web/    alternative grouping for cost comparison

sections.title: Put dependencies in the packages that use them
sections.body:
The existing fixture inherits paths from the workspace. For your own workspace, define the registry dependencies below in its root `Cargo.toml` and inherit them in member packages.

The descriptor crate uses islands and serde; the native site uses server and islands; a browser unit enables dom/islands on fusor and browser on fusor-islands. Keep each unit’s generated HTML setup and build dependency as in a normal app.
sections.language: Cargo.toml · root of a separate workspace
sections.note: In the browser member’s `[dependencies]`, use `fusor-core = { workspace = true, features = ["islands"] }` and `fusor-islands = { workspace = true, features = ["browser"] }`. The setting `workspace = true` requires those dependencies to be defined in the workspace manifest.

sections.title: Define what Cart means
sections.body:
`Cart` here is a descriptor, not the `CartView` state type that owns the template.

Its associated `Props` type defines the serialized input; `UNIT` selects a separately compiled browser package, and `SCHEMA` names the props contract.

The default mode attaches to matching native HTML. The full fixture defines `Designer` with an explicit Preview mode as well.
sections.note: A descriptor is a small Rust type that identifies the feature across the native renderer and browser bundle. It does not own the UI state. `CartView` owns the template and signals. For named tag inputs, `Props` is a struct with public named fields; rustc checks the supplied fields and their types.

sections.title: Connect native and browser implementations
sections.body:
`fusor-server` renders resolved data into HTML in native Rust; it does not require an HTTP framework.

The site registers `Cart` with a `CartView` factory and renders using a manifest plus that registry. cart-web exports the corresponding browser factory below.

The delivery metadata maps the unit name cart to that Cargo package. This is extra package setup, not an attribute that automatically splits an ordinary app.
sections.note: The native site executable implements the CLI render protocol; copying this registration alone is not a complete native app. Use the linked executable and manifest as the working starting point. Unit registration stays side-effect free; activation constructs state.

sections.title: Control an island from already active Rust
sections.body:
An active component can look up an island by descriptor and instance id.

The methods below belong inside an async task started after that caller’s owner activates. The handle uses the same loader as HTML policies.

Lookup/status do not download code. A dropped waiter or disposed caller cancels its wait; it does not dispose an already active target.
sections.language: Rust · inside an active caller’s async task
sections.note: Add `hydrate:id="cart-42"` to that `Cart` tag to make this lookup work.

sections.title: Communicate between active islands
sections.body:
`fusor_islands::browser::emit::<Descriptor, Payload>` sends an explicitly named message with a serializable payload. `browser::listen::<Descriptor, Payload>` registers an owner-scoped listener that decodes it.

The receiver decides how to update its own signals.

Messages do not carry signal handles and do not `hydrate` a sleeping receiver. Put shared, tightly coupled reactive state inside one island instead of treating events as shared memory.
sections.note: Listeners are cleaned up with their owner. The payload types must agree between sender and receiver; the descriptor identifies the event namespace. The linked API source contains the exact signatures and lifecycle rules.

links.label: Typed island event and control APIs

title: Native JavaScript and npm
lead: Bring a browser library into your app using its normal JavaScript API. Learn where the code lives, how Rust and JavaScript exchange values, and who cleans up when a component disappears.

sections.title: The connection, independent of the library
sections.body:
fusor compiles your Rust state and HTML into a browser application. A JavaScript module can run alongside that component. Rust owns the application state; JavaScript calls the library.

Rust sends selected values through read-only inputs, and JavaScript reports results through ordinary DOM events. You do not need a Rust wrapper for each package.

JavaScript is optional: a utility can run without Rust inputs or events, and a widget can run without reactive state.
sections.code:
Rust signal → JavaScript input → library call
Library result or event → DOM CustomEvent → Rust handler → updated HTML

links.label: New to Fusor? Start with a browser app
A signal is a value the page watches

sections.title: First, check the library’s browser API
sections.body:
A function library can be imported and called directly. A chart, map, editor, or other stateful widget fits when its browser API lets you choose a host element and release its resources.

An existing Web `Component` fits through its native custom tag.

Look for the package’s browser import, initialization, update, events, and destroy/dispose instructions; those remain the library’s API, not fusor APIs.
sections.note:
Installing an npm package does not make every package browser-compatible. Node-only APIs such as fs are not provided.

React-only components still require React’s own runtime and mounting API inside a dedicated host; they do not become fusor component tags.

This integration currently targets client-rendered browser components. Server-rendered modes and coordinated `<Async>` regions are outside its scope; see the full release boundaries below for exact restrictions and supported npm layouts.

sections.title: Enable JavaScript once per application
sections.body:
After installing the fusor CLI and its browser tools, create an app with --javascript.

The flag enables the Rust feature, adds the pinned esbuild build tool, and connects `web/app.js` to the app HTML.

Run these commands wherever you keep projects; the command creates the `my-app` directory. If you already have an app, follow the next section instead.
sections.code:
fusor new my-app --javascript
cd my-app
fusor dev
sections.note: Node 22+ is required for JavaScript browser builds. Commit `package.json` and the version-3 `package-lock.json`; use `npm ci` on subsequent installations. Cargo does not install npm packages. Native `cargo check` remains Node-free.

links.label: Install the CLI and browser tools

sections.title: Already have an app?
sections.body:
Run `fusor add javascript` in your app to enable the Rust feature and prepare pinned esbuild dependencies. Existing sources and features are preserved. Use Node 22+ for JavaScript browser builds. Commit the updated manifests and lockfiles.

Create `web/app.js`. Add `<script type="module" src="./app.js"></script>` directly inside the existing `<App>`, beside its native root, as shown below. Keep `build.rs` calling `fusor_build::compile_app()`.
sections.code: fusor add javascript
sections.note: A Cargo feature enables optional Rust code in a dependency. You enable this feature once per app, not once per library. If this checkout uses a local path dependency, preserve that path.

sections.title: Repeat this pattern for each library
sections.body: Install the package from your app’s Cargo directory, beside `Cargo.toml`: npm install --save-exact PACKAGE (replace PACKAGE with the package name). Import it in your module using the import path documented by its author. Then choose only the connections you need:
sections.code:
1. Put per-instance setup in onMount.
2. If the library draws UI, give it a dedicated host inside root.
3. If it needs Rust state, expose a signal and subscribe to that input.
4. If Rust needs a result, dispatch a CustomEvent on root.
5. If it creates resources, register their cleanup immediately.
sections.note: Create a stateful library instance once inside `onMount`, then update that instance in subscriptions. Creating it inside every subscription callback would recreate it on each change. One component module can import multiple libraries and helper modules; a separate wrapper component is optional.

sections.title: What onMount receives
sections.body:
fusor calls `onMount` with one context object when this component instance becomes active in the page and its Rust event handlers are ready.

The `{ root, inputs, signal, onCleanup }` syntax is ordinary JavaScript object destructuring: it takes four named properties from that one argument. You can take only the properties you need; you do not construct or pass the context yourself.
sections.note: This is a fusor calling convention for an ordinary named JavaScript export. Top-level imports/code run once per module URL; `onMount` runs separately for each instance. Rust `signal` changes and keyed moves do not rerun it. You can omit `onMount` for a module that only imports a Web `Component` registration.

links.label: Use the generated types in your editor

sections.title: The types inside the context
sections.body:
`root` is the component’s native DOM `Element`, such as its `<main>` or `<section>`. It is not the `<App>` marker or a Rust value.

`inputs` contains the read-only Rust values this component exposes to JavaScript. Each connection provides `get()` for a snapshot and `subscribe()` for updates.

`signal` is a browser `AbortSignal` tied to the component’s lifetime. It is unrelated to the Rust `Signal<T>` type.

`onCleanup` accepts a function with no arguments and registers it to run during cleanup. It returns nothing. The `onMount` function must be synchronous and cannot return a `Promise`. For deferred work, use the async setup pattern later in this guide.

The generated type contract below shows all four properties together.
sections.language: TypeScript · Generated contract, not code you need to write
sections.note:
`T` is an input’s value type; `I` is this component’s exposed input object. Here `inputs.text.get()` returns a string. The callback passed to `subscribe` receives a string; `subscribe` returns an unsubscribe function. Unmarked Rust fields are absent; `inputs` is empty when no fields are exposed.

`readonly` prevents replacing context properties. The DOM element itself remains mutable. Since `querySelector` can return `null`, check `instanceof HTMLCanvasElement` before passing a selected node to a canvas API.

Use `signal.aborted` to detect removal, or pass `signal` to `fetch` and `addEventListener`. Register destruction with `onCleanup(() => widget.destroy())`.

sections.title: A small complete connection
sections.body:
The following example uses a tiny function package so you can see Rust → JavaScript → Rust without chart configuration.

In your generated app, run npm install --save-exact is-lower-case@2.0.2. Add `web-sys` = "=0.3.94" under `Cargo.toml`’s existing `[dependencies]`; it supplies the Rust browser Event type used by the return handler.

Replace the three files below. Keep the generated app’s `src/lib.rs`, `build.rs`, and other files unchanged.
sections.code:
my-app/
  Cargo.toml          Rust dependencies and JavaScript feature
  package.json        npm library and esbuild
  package-lock.json   committed npm versions
  src/app.rs          Rust state and return-event handler
  web/index.html      HTML and module association
  web/app.js          ordinary library import and call
sections.note: `web-sys` is needed here because Rust receives a browser event; a JavaScript-only library call does not need this Rust event handler. This example does not require a child component or a `FromInputs` implementation.

sections.title: Rust: choose which state JavaScript can read
sections.body:
`App` is an ordinary Rust struct holding the page’s state. `Signal<String>` is a reactive text value; `Signal<bool>` holds true or false.

`#[derive(JsInputs)]` asks Rust to generate the JavaScript input interface. Only the `#[js]` field text is exposed. `is_lowercase` stays in Rust and receives the checked result.

`new()` supplies initial values; `"rust".into()` creates an owned Rust `String`.
sections.note: event_detail::`<bool>`(&event) asks for a boolean payload. `Result` represents success or failure; `if let Ok(value)` handles only a valid payload. `template!("web/index.html")` associates this Rust module with that HTML file. The event connection is shown next.

sections.title: HTML: place the module at its component boundary
sections.body:
The script is a direct child of `App`, next to its one native root, main. Its `src` is relative to this HTML file.

In a reusable component, put the script directly inside `<template rust:component="YourType">` in the same way.

fusor extracts the script and calls its lifecycle export; it does not leave an inert script inside each cloned template.
sections.code: All lowercase: {{ state.is_lowercase.get() }}
sections.note: `App::new()` constructs the Rust value, and state means that value inside this HTML. `bind` keeps the input and `state.text` in sync. `on:library-result` calls the Rust method when main receives an event named `library-result`; event is supplied by the framework. JavaScript root is this same main element.

sections.title: JavaScript: call the package normally
sections.body:
The import and isLowerCase(text) call come from the package’s JavaScript API. subscribe receives the current text immediately, then later Rust changes.

The callback reports the boolean on root; Rust updates `is_lowercase`, and the HTML output changes.

Save all three files, then run `fusor dev`. The initial word rust shows true; type Rust to see false.
sections.note: For a different function library, change the import and call. Match the exposed Rust input and result type to its data. This utility owns no timer or UI instance to destroy; the framework stops its input subscription when the component is removed. No cleanup stack or custom adapter is required for this case.

sections.title: Rust → JavaScript: snapshots and subscriptions
sections.body:
`inputs.text.get()` reads the current value once; it does not keep a variable updated. `inputs.text.subscribe(callback)` immediately delivers that value and then follows changes.

It returns a function you can call to unsubscribe early. All subscriptions stop when this component is disposed (removed or replaced).

Notifications follow a Rust reactive batch: for example, the grouped state writes made by one event handler. JavaScript inputs have no `set` method.
sections.note:
Supported `Signal` values are `bool`, `String`, `f64`, `i32`, `u32`, and nested `Option`/Vec combinations. `Vec` is a Rust array-like collection, sent as a JS array snapshot; `Option` is an optional value, with `None` sent as null. Mutating a snapshot does not write back to Rust.

Advanced callers may expose `JsValue` handles, which retain JS identity. Arbitrary Rust structs and 64-bit integers are not converted automatically.

Subscribe to separate inputs separately; this is not an atomic snapshot of several fields.

sections.title: JavaScript → Rust: match the event name and payload
sections.body:
Choose your own event name. `new CustomEvent("library-result", { detail: result })` matches `on:library-result` in HTML.

The Rust handler receives a `web_sys::Event`, then event_detail::`<bool>`(&event) validates its payload. Change `bool` to a supported type such as `String` when your library returns text.

Invalid types return an error; application-specific checks, such as whether an ID exists, are still yours.
sections.language: JavaScript · Dispatch from a library callback
sections.note: Dispatching on `root` reaches the listener on that same element; bubbling is unnecessary. Dispatching from a descendant requires `bubbles: true` to reach a `root` listener. Use the library’s callback/event API to trigger this dispatch. A module cannot call an arbitrary Rust method by its JavaScript name; the HTML event handler makes that connection explicit.

links.label: Events: browser handlers and custom messages

sections.title: Give a widget its own empty element
sections.body:
For a chart, map, or editor, add an empty host inside main alongside your fusor controls.

A data attribute gives JavaScript a way to find that element within this component instance, without a global ID. Use a canvas instead if the library requires one.
sections.note: fusor owns the host element and the surrounding page; the library owns the contents it creates inside the host. Keep fusor child components and interpolations outside that library-managed subtree.

sections.title: For a widget, separate DOM ownership and lifetime
sections.body:
Give a library an empty host element, or a canvas, inside your component’s root. fusor renders the surrounding controls; the library manages that host’s contents.

Do not put fusor-managed children or interpolations inside a subtree the library will replace.

Find the host with `root.querySelector`, initialize the library once, update it from subscriptions, and call its documented destroy/dispose method through `onCleanup`.
sections.language: JavaScript · Use with the host above
sections.note: `ResizeObserver` is a browser API, not an npm package or a fusor wrapper. Replace this resource with your library’s documented initialization and release calls. There is no universal `destroy()` method. The linked `Chart.js` and `Three.js` modules demonstrate actual library APIs.

links.label: Three.js: renderer, animation and GPU cleanup

sections.title: What cleanup does automatically
sections.body:
When a component is removed, its JavaScript input subscriptions close, `signal` aborts, and registered cleanups run in reverse registration order while `root` is still available.

Pass `{ signal }` to native addEventListener or fetch to tie supported work to that lifetime.

Register explicit cleanup immediately for timers, observers, animation loops, and library resources; aborting does not destroy those automatically. A returned cleanup function is also allowed.
sections.note:
Registering cleanup after disposal runs it immediately. If synchronous `onMount` throws, already registered cleanups still run; one failing cleanup does not skip the rest.

fusor reports the error, but does not automatically retry or undo arbitrary library DOM changes. A component prepared but never activated does not run `onMount`.

sections.title: Optional: load a library only when needed
sections.body:
Start with a static import unless you want deferred loading. You can replace `web/app.js` with the version below to defer this utility until the component mounts.

`onMount` must remain synchronous: an async `onMount` or returned `Promise` is an error.

Start `Promise` work inside it, check `signal.aborted` after awaiting/loading, and catch failures. Dynamic import itself cannot be cancelled; the check prevents installing work after removal.
sections.note: For async setup that acquires a chart, renderer, or several resources, also release partially acquired work if the `Promise` fails. Framework cleanup catches synchronous setup failure; it cannot catch arbitrary future `Promise` callbacks. The showcases explain this extra case with a local idempotent cleanup stack used both in catch and `onCleanup`. That stack is application JavaScript, not required boilerplate for every library.

links.label: Async initialization and rollback in a real widget

sections.title: Imports, TypeScript, and editor help
sections.body:
Use external `.js`, `.mjs`, or `.ts` modules, or an inline module body. Relative imports resolve from that module; bare package imports resolve installed npm dependencies. Follow the package’s documentation for import names and options. CSS and file assets can be imported too.

Dynamic imports split JavaScript into separate files. Linked CSS loads with the page. Apps with component JavaScript currently rebuild and reload on source edits, including HTML and CSS changes; ordinary reactive input updates keep the existing library instance.

A browser CLI build generates `.fusor/types/` declarations for the associated Rust state. Build once before adding the annotation, and rebuild after changing `#[js]` fields. Import the generated type so its inputs stay aligned with your Rust fields.

The JSDoc annotation and `@ts-check` enable editor diagnostics without adding runtime code. For TypeScript, rename `app.js` to `app.ts`, update the HTML `src`, and use `import type { AppMountContext } from "../.fusor/types/web-index-html-App";`. Annotate the argument as `context: AppMountContext` and the return as `void | (() => void)`.

`esbuild` transpiles TypeScript but does not type-check it. Configure and run `tsc --noEmit` separately if desired. Native `cargo check` does not resolve JavaScript imports.

sections.title: Existing Web Components use their native tags
sections.body:
An existing custom element is already a browser component; it does not need a Rust struct or a fusor PascalCase wrapper.

Install its package, add the author’s registration import to your existing module, and use its native HTML tag.

For example, after npm install --save-exact @shoelace-style/shoelace@2.20.1, add import "@`shoelace-style/shoelace/dist/components/button/button.js`"; to `web/app.js` and put this tag inside main:
sections.code:
<sl-button prop:disabled="{{ state.is_lowercase.get() }}">
  An existing Web Component
</sl-button>
sections.note: Here `disabled` is a JavaScript property: `true` disables the button. Attribute interpolation is text; `prop:name` passes an actual value and waits for custom-element definition. Event/property suffixes preserve case. `Registration` is shared, while each native tag is its own element. There is still only one component module script; add imports to it. If the library documents a required stylesheet, import it in the same module too.

sections.title: Troubleshooting and current boundaries
sections.body:
If an import is missing, install the package in this app’s Cargo directory and run the browser CLI build.

If `inputs` lacks a field, check the `javascript` feature, `JsInputs` derive, and `#[js]` annotation, then rebuild. If a value changes only once, use `subscribe` instead of reading once with `get`.

If Rust never receives an event, check its exact name, dispatch target, bubbling, and payload type. If a widget resets on every update, create it once in `onMount` rather than inside the subscription callback.
sections.note:
Current scope: client-rendered browser templates, one native root and at most one module declaration per component, one JavaScript-enabled fusor app per page. Server/shared/island and coherent templates reject component JavaScript.

Module discovery covers the application package, not dependent Cargo crates.

Builds require package-local npm manifests, a version-3 lock and installed dependencies; npm workspaces, linked packages and other package-manager layouts are not supported. Rust-only apps do not need Node or this bridge.

sections.title: Place a module in a reusable component
sections.body:
A reusable component can own its JavaScript module just as the application root does. Put the module script directly inside its `template` declaration, beside the native root. The module receives that instance’s root and lifetime in `onMount`.

The `LibraryPanel` Rust type must be associated with this HTML and implement the normal component construction contract. Its caller then uses `<LibraryPanel></LibraryPanel>` wherever the integration is needed.
sections.language: HTML · LibraryPanel is your component type
sections.note: Use `onCleanup` to destroy library instances and release subscriptions. `JsInputs` is needed when the module receives Rust inputs; DOM events carry results back to Rust.

links.label: Define the Rust state and reusable HTML

sections.title: Make it reusable when your app needs it
sections.body:
The example used `App` to avoid component plumbing. To reuse an integration, move its Rust state, HTML host and module into a normal fusor component and use its tag wherever needed.

`JsInputs` exposes state to that component’s JavaScript; `FromInputs` is the separate contract for values passed by its Rust parent. Neither is a library-specific adapter API.

Start directly in `App`, or make a component immediately when reuse is useful.
